screens.title: What is NAT and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Network Address Translation is the process of rewriting IP address information in packet headers while packets traverse a routing device. At a minimum, NAT alters either the source or destination IP address field to map private address space to public address space or vice versa. Practically, NAT exists because public IPv4 addresses are limited; without NAT every device would need its own public address. A simple example: a host with 192.168.10.10 requests a web page. When the packet leaves the private network, the NAT device changes the source IP to a public address, so the remote server replies to that public address. The NAT device keeps a small state table to map the return traffic back to the internal host. A common misconception is that NAT alone provides security; while it hides internal addresses, explicit security policies are still required on Junos to permit translated traffic. Another misconception is that NAT always changes both source and destination; it changes only the field you configure. Takeaway: NAT is a stateful header transformation that conserves public IPs and enables controlled exposure of internal services. Ask yourself: which field should I change for this design — source for outbound sharing, destination for port forwarding, or a static one-to-one mapping?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: NAT rewrites source or destination IP headers so private networks can communicate with public networks while preserving address space.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is NAT and why it matters
Definition

NAT remaps one IP address space into another by modifying IP header addresses of passing packets. It is stateful and records translations for returning traffic.

Packet example
Original: src=192.168.10.10 dst=198.51.100.20. After SNAT: src=203.0.113.10 dst=198.51.100.20. Return traffic arrives to 203.0.113.10 and NAT maps it back to 192.168.10.10.
Why it matters
Conserves public IPv4 and lets private hosts use shared addresses for internet access.
Misconception
NAT is not a substitute for security policies; Junos requires explicit policies to permit translated flows.
Concrete analogy
Think of NAT as a mail forwarding service. Outbound mail is stamped with a shared public address; replies arrive there and the service forwards them internally to the correct private recipient.
Quick bullets
  • Operates on packet headers to remap IP addresses.
  • May be many-to-one (SNAT), one-to-many (pool), or one-to-one (static).
  • Stateful mapping is required to reverse translations for replies.
Key Takeaway

NAT changes only the address fields you configure; choose source, destination, or static mapping for the intended traffic flow.

screens.title: Types of NAT: SNAT, DNAT, and Static NAT
screens.narratorSegment: There are three primary NAT types you will use on Junos: Source NAT, Destination NAT, and Static NAT. Source NAT modifies the source IP of packets leaving a private network so internal hosts can reach public networks; interface NAT and pool NAT are common SNAT variants. Interface NAT maps outgoing traffic to the address of the egress interface and typically relies on port numbers for multiplexing. Pool NAT translates to addresses chosen from a predefined public pool. Destination NAT changes the destination IP and optionally the port of incoming packets so external clients can reach an internal server; this is commonly called port forwarding. Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between a private host and a public IP, useful for servers that must be consistently reachable. A frequent design question is which type to use: choose SNAT when internal users only need outbound access, DNAT when you must expose a service with controlled ports, and Static NAT when a persistent public identity is required. Misunderstanding these roles leads to excessive exposure or broken connectivity. As you plan NAT, think through the direction of traffic and which header field needs translation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Types of NAT
Source NAT (SNAT)
Translates the source IP of outbound packets so private hosts share public addresses.
Variants
Interface NAT: maps to egress interface IP and uses ports for multiplexing. Pool NAT: assigns public addresses from a configurable pool to distribute load.
Destination NAT (DNAT)
Maps incoming public destination IP/port to an internal private server and port.
Typical use
Expose a web server on a public IP and forward port 80 to an internal IP.
Static NAT
Permanent one-to-one mapping between private and public IPs for servers requiring fixed public addresses.
When to use
Use for services that must be consistently reachable and do not benefit from port translation.
Decision guide
  • Need outbound internet for many hosts with few public IPs → SNAT (interface or pool).
  • Need to allow external clients to reach internal server on specific ports → DNAT (port forwarding).
  • Need a permanent public address for a server → Static NAT.
Common mistake
Exposing more ports than necessary in DNAT increases attack surface. Always limit destination matches to required ports and, when possible, restrict source addresses.

screens.title: Source NAT deep dive — Interface NAT (PAT/NAPT)
screens.narratorSegment: Interface NAT, commonly called PAT or NAPT, is a form of Source NAT where many internal hosts share the IP address assigned to the egress interface. The mechanism relies on port numbers to distinguish concurrent connections. When an internal host sends a packet, the SRX replaces the source IP with the interface IP and rewrites the source port as necessary. The device records the mapping of original source IP and port to translated source IP and port so return traffic can be matched to the correct internal host. A practical example: multiple hosts in 192.168.10.0/24 all appear to the internet as 203.0.113.10, but their outbound TCP connections use different ephemeral source ports. A common misconception is that NAT always preserves source ports; in high-port-collision situations the device will remap ports. This is normal. When designing capacity, remember that interface NAT multiplexes thousands of connections but may hit port exhaustion in extremely heavy environments. Key verification after applying an interface-nat rule-set is to generate outbound traffic and check the active mapping via show security flow session and show security nat source persistent-nat to confirm translations exist and are reversing correctly.

keyIdea.title: Interface NAT
keyIdea.text: Interface NAT maps many private hosts to the egress interface IP and uses port numbers to keep connections distinct.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Interface NAT (PAT/NAPT)
Step-by-step flow
1. Packet exits private host
2. Router replaces src IP with egress interface IP
3. Port rewrite and state recorded
Interface NAT relies on the combination of translated source IP and source port to create unique mappings. The NAT device maintains a table so that returning packets are translated back to the original internal source IP and port.
Key Takeaway

Interface NAT is efficient for many hosts but relies on port space; monitor session counts to avoid port exhaustion.

Common mistake
Assuming source ports are preserved and not checking for collisions during heavy outbound connection loads.
Concrete example
Three hosts in 192.168.10.0/24 open connections to different web servers. The SRX replaces each source IP with 203.0.113.10 and assigns distinct ephemeral source ports so replies return correctly to each host.
Verification commands
After generating traffic: show security nat source persistent-nat; show security flow session. These show active translations and session mappings.
Pro tip
When you expect many concurrent sessions, monitor session counts and plan for pool NAT or additional public addresses to avoid port depletion.

screens.title: Pool NAT and when to use it
screens.narratorSegment: Pool NAT is another flavor of Source NAT where the NAT device translates private source addresses to addresses drawn from a predefined pool of public IPs. This differs from interface NAT where all hosts share a single egress IP; pool NAT gives you more public addresses so you can distribute translations and reduce the chance of port exhaustion per address. An example scenario is an organization with a small block of public IPs that wants to spread outbound translation across those addresses for capacity or policy reasons. In Junos you define a source rule-set that matches traffic and then specify a source-nat pool instead of interface. A common misconception is that pool NAT provides privacy or security benefits beyond address diversity; it mainly affects capacity and how remote servers see your origin addresses. When troubleshooting, ensure your match conditions (such as source-address) accurately reflect the internal networks you intended to translate. If you forget to restrict matches, you may accidentally translate traffic you did not intend to, which complicates logging and tracing. Pool NAT and when to use it means pool nat maps internal addresses to a range of public ips for better scaling and distribution of outbound traffic.. In practical terms, distributing translations across multiple public ip addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Pool NAT maps internal addresses to a range of public IPs for better scaling and distribution of outbound traffic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Pool NAT
What pool NAT does
Selects public addresses from a configured pool to translate private source IPs, distributing outbound load across multiple public IPs.
When to choose pool NAT
  • When a single interface IP risks port exhaustion.
  • When you want remote servers to see different origin IPs for distribution, logging, or policy reasons.
Design note and caution
Pool NAT scales capacity but can complicate access control on remote services if those services expect a single origin IP. Also ensure logging and monitoring account for multiple translated addresses.
Practical tip

Document the pool ranges so that security teams and external services can whitelist expected public IPs if required.

screens.title: Destination NAT (DNAT) — Port forwarding explained
screens.narratorSegment: Destination NAT, often called port forwarding, changes the destination IP and optionally the destination port of incoming packets so external users reach an internal server. A common use case is exposing a web server in a DMZ: external clients connect to a public IP on port 80, and the NAT device translates that destination to the internal web server's private IP and port. It's important to pair DNAT with a security policy that permits the translated destination; NAT alone does not open a path. For example, if you translate 203.0.113.5:80 to 192.168.1.10:80, you still need a Junos policy from the untrust zone to the dmz zone that allows HTTP to 192.168.1.10. A common misconception is to use source-address any in DNAT rules; restricting match conditions by destination-port and destination-address reduces exposure. Also, be precise with zones; misconfigured from/to zones prevents the DNAT rule from being applied. After configuration, verify translations with show security nat destination and inspect sessions with show security flow session to confirm the translation and policy match. Destination NAT (DNAT) — Port forwarding explained means dnat forwards external destination addresses and ports to internal servers; always pair dnat with an appropriate security policy.. In practical terms, mapping public ip and port to an internal server. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DNAT essence
keyIdea.text: DNAT forwards external destination addresses and ports to internal servers; always pair DNAT with an appropriate security policy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Destination NAT (DNAT)
How DNAT works

DNAT matches incoming traffic based on destination address and port, then rewrites that destination to the internal server address and port, enabling external access to private services.

Security requirement
After DNAT, create a security policy from the external zone to the internal zone allowing traffic to the translated private address. Without this policy the flow will be dropped.
Configuration note
Be specific in DNAT matches: include the public destination IP and the exact port to avoid unintentionally exposing services.
Key Takeaway

DNAT exposes services by translating destination addresses; pair it with a restrictive security policy to minimize attack surface.

Common mistake
Forgetting to allow the translated destination in a policy, or using too-broad destination matches that expose extra services.

screens.title: Static NAT: one-to-one mappings
screens.narratorSegment: Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between a private IP and a public IP. This is useful for servers that must be consistently reachable at an unchanging public address, such as mail or legacy systems that rely on fixed source IPs. Because the mapping is static, there is no port translation by default; the public IP is always mapped to the same private host. A typical mistake is to use static NAT for hosts that could instead be protected behind DNAT and selective port forwarding; static NAT increases exposure because the mapped public address resolves directly to the internal host. When configuring static NAT on Junos, ensure access is limited by security policy and that DNS and external services are updated to reference the assigned public address. Verify mappings with show security nat destination for DNAT-like scenarios or by checking the NAT rule-set and confirming traffic flows using show security flow session after initiating connections. Static NAT: one-to-one mappings means static nat gives a fixed public identity to a private host; use it when a consistent, dedicated public address is required.. In practical terms, permanent mappings for servers needing consistent public addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Static mapping
keyIdea.text: Static NAT gives a fixed public identity to a private host; use it when a consistent, dedicated public address is required.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Static NAT
Use case
Assign a stable public IP to a server that external clients must reach reliably, for example a mail gateway or an externally-visible application.
Design caution
Static NAT exposes the internal host at the mapped public address without port translation by default. Ensure policies and host hardening are in place before assigning a static mapping.
Checklist
  • Confirm required public IP is available.
  • Document mapping and update DNS if needed.
  • Verify with show security flow session after traffic.
Quick tip

Prefer DNAT for selective services; reserve Static NAT where a fixed public identity is mandatory.

screens.title: Configuring Source NAT (Interface NAT) on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the exact Junos configuration needed to implement Source NAT using interface NAT. Start in configuration mode and define a source-nat rule-set that matches traffic from the internal trust zone to the external untrust zone. Within that rule-set create a rule that matches your internal source network and specifies source-nat interface as the translation action. After committing, generate outbound traffic from an internal host and verify with show security nat source rule-set to see the configured rule and show security flow session to observe active translations. A common configuration error is mismatching zones in the rule-set. If the rule-set from/to zones are wrong, NAT will not be applied to the traffic. Another mistake is forgetting the security policy from trust to untrust allowing the traffic; NAT alone does not permit flows. Use the following template as provided, substitute your interfaces and networks, commit, then verify active NAT entries. As a learning check, ask yourself: can I see the internal source rewritten to the interface IP in the active flow output? Configuring Source NAT (Interface NAT) on Junos means use a source-nat rule-set with a rule that specifies source-nat interface, then verify with show security nat source and flow session commands.. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Configuring Source NAT
Junos configuration template
# Enter configuration mode
edit

# 1. Define the NAT rule set
set security nat source rule-set trust-to-untrust from zone trust
set security nat source rule-set trust-to-untrust to zone untrust

# 2. Create a rule within the rule set
set security nat source rule-set trust-to-untrust rule interface-nat match source-address 0.0.0.0/0
set security nat source rule-set trust-to-untrust rule interface-nat then source-nat interface

# Commit the changes
commit and-quit
Verification
  • show security nat source rule-set trust-to-untrust
  • show security nat source persistent-nat (after traffic)
  • show security flow session (to see active translated sessions)
Common mistake
Not creating or enabling a security policy from trust to untrust. NAT without a policy still results in blocked traffic.
Concrete example
Internal network 192.168.10.0/24 in zone trust needs internet access via untrust interface with a public IP. The sample configuration above sets interface NAT for all sources in that zone.
Key Takeaway

After committing your NAT rule-set, generate traffic and use flow and nat show commands to validate active translation entries.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Configuring Destination NAT
Junos DNAT template
# Enter configuration mode
edit

# 1. Define the NAT rule set for incoming traffic
set security nat destination rule-set untrust-to-dmz from zone untrust
set security nat destination rule-set untrust-to-dmz to zone dmz

# 2. Create a rule within the rule set
set security nat destination rule-set untrust-to-dmz rule web-server-access match destination-address 203.0.113.5
set security nat destination rule-set untrust-to-dmz rule web-server-access match destination-port 80

# 3. Specify the translation
set security nat destination rule-set untrust-to-dmz rule web-server-access then destination-nat to address 192.168.1.10 port 80

# Commit the changes
commit and-quit
Security policy reminder
Add a policy from-zone untrust to-zone dmz allowing application http to destination-address 192.168.1.10. NAT does not bypass policy checks.
Verification
  • show security nat destination
  • show security flow session (to view the translated destination in active sessions)
Concrete scenario
Web server at 192.168.1.10 in dmz should be reachable at 203.0.113.5:80 from the Internet. Configure DNAT and the matching policy, then test from an external client.

A DNAT rule and an explicit security policy are both required to expose internal services safely and successfully.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap three foundational NAT concepts you will rely on. First, NAT remaps IP address fields in packet headers so private networks can reach public networks and vice versa; it is a stateful process that must remember mappings to reverse translations. Second, Source NAT changes the source address for outbound traffic; Interface NAT (PAT) is the many-to-one pattern that uses the egress interface IP and port multiplexing, while pool NAT selects from multiple public IPs. Keep these three ideas in mind when designing NAT rules and policies: direction of change, the field being translated, and the security policy requirement. Network Address Translation (NAT)
Remaps IP address information in packet headers to enable private-to-public communication while tracking state for return traffic.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: Here are six concise facts to keep at your fingertips while you design or troubleshoot NAT on Junos. Interface NAT uses the egress interface IP and port multiplexing. Pool NAT distributes outbound translations across a set of public addresses. Static NAT creates a fixed one-to-one mapping for services that need a stable public identity. DNAT is used for port forwarding external requests to internal servers and always needs a security policy from the external zone to the internal zone. Finally, avoid overly broad DNAT matches; restrict destination addresses and ports to minimize exposure. These quick reminders will help you configure NAT correctly and keep your network predictable and secure.

fullNarratorScript:
Network Address Translation is one of those practical technologies that keeps networks reachable and secure while conserving scarce public IPv4 addresses. In this chapter you will learn what NAT does at a packet level, why organizations use Source, Destination and Static NAT, and the concrete Junos configuration steps to make each type work. You'll see how interface NAT lets many private hosts share a single public address, how pool NAT distributes translations across several public IPs, and how destination NAT forwards service traffic from a public address to a private server. We will also walk through common verification commands and troubleshooting checks you will use in daily operations. By the end you will be able to explain when to use SNAT versus DNAT, write Junos rule-sets for each, and avoid the most frequent mistakes such as missing security policies or incorrect zone matches. Think of this chapter as the practical bridge between private networks and the public Internet — you will leave able to configure, validate, and explain NAT with confidence.

In this first objectives panel we will frame the four core skills you gain. First, you will explain why NAT exists and what it changes in an IP packet header. That means understanding both address conservation and how NAT can reduce exposure of internal IPs. Second, you will differentiate SNAT, DNAT, and Static NAT — that is, you will be able to name each type, describe what part of the packet is changed, and give a short example of when to use it. Third, you will configure Source NAT on Junos devices, including interface NAT so internal hosts access the internet, and pool NAT when multiple public IPs are available. You will practice writing rule-sets and rules in Junos configuration mode. Fourth, you will configure Destination NAT to expose internal services securely and understand the associated security policy requirements. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify you configured NAT correctly and validated translations with the recommended show commands.

This second objectives screen focuses on how you will practice and verify the skills. For explaining NAT, you will trace packet headers through a NAT device and state exactly which fields change, reinforcing why conserving public addresses matters. For differentiating types, you will match real scenarios to SNAT, DNAT and Static NAT so you can choose the right tool in design decisions. For configuring Source NAT you will implement an interface NAT rule-set on a Junos SRX, commit it, generate traffic, and use show security nat source and show security flow session to confirm translations. For Destination NAT you will configure a DNAT rule mapping a public IP and port to an internal server, then confirm translated destination addresses and ensure a security policy from untrust to dmz permits the flow. Each card ends with a verified competency milestone so you know which commands prove your work. Practicing with these verification steps prevents the common mistake of assuming NAT works without checking active sessions.

Network Address Translation is the process of rewriting IP address information in packet headers while packets traverse a routing device. At a minimum, NAT alters either the source or destination IP address field to map private address space to public address space or vice versa. Practically, NAT exists because public IPv4 addresses are limited; without NAT every device would need its own public address. A simple example: a host with 192.168.10.10 requests a web page. When the packet leaves the private network, the NAT device changes the source IP to a public address, so the remote server replies to that public address. The NAT device keeps a small state table to map the return traffic back to the internal host. A common misconception is that NAT alone provides security; while it hides internal addresses, explicit security policies are still required on Junos to permit translated traffic. Another misconception is that NAT always changes both source and destination; it changes only the field you configure. Takeaway: NAT is a stateful header transformation that conserves public IPs and enables controlled exposure of internal services. Ask yourself: which field should I change for this design — source for outbound sharing, destination for port forwarding, or a static one-to-one mapping?

There are three primary NAT types you will use on Junos: Source NAT, Destination NAT, and Static NAT. Source NAT modifies the source IP of packets leaving a private network so internal hosts can reach public networks; interface NAT and pool NAT are common SNAT variants. Interface NAT maps outgoing traffic to the address of the egress interface and typically relies on port numbers for multiplexing. Pool NAT translates to addresses chosen from a predefined public pool. Destination NAT changes the destination IP and optionally the port of incoming packets so external clients can reach an internal server; this is commonly called port forwarding. Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between a private host and a public IP, useful for servers that must be consistently reachable. A frequent design question is which type to use: choose SNAT when internal users only need outbound access, DNAT when you must expose a service with controlled ports, and Static NAT when a persistent public identity is required. Misunderstanding these roles leads to excessive exposure or broken connectivity. As you plan NAT, think through the direction of traffic and which header field needs translation.

Interface NAT, commonly called PAT or NAPT, is a form of Source NAT where many internal hosts share the IP address assigned to the egress interface. The mechanism relies on port numbers to distinguish concurrent connections. When an internal host sends a packet, the SRX replaces the source IP with the interface IP and rewrites the source port as necessary. The device records the mapping of original source IP and port to translated source IP and port so return traffic can be matched to the correct internal host. A practical example: multiple hosts in 192.168.10.0/24 all appear to the internet as 203.0.113.10, but their outbound TCP connections use different ephemeral source ports. A common misconception is that NAT always preserves source ports; in high-port-collision situations the device will remap ports. This is normal. When designing capacity, remember that interface NAT multiplexes thousands of connections but may hit port exhaustion in extremely heavy environments. Key verification after applying an interface-nat rule-set is to generate outbound traffic and check the active mapping via show security flow session and show security nat source persistent-nat to confirm translations exist and are reversing correctly.

Pool NAT is another flavor of Source NAT where the NAT device translates private source addresses to addresses drawn from a predefined pool of public IPs. This differs from interface NAT where all hosts share a single egress IP; pool NAT gives you more public addresses so you can distribute translations and reduce the chance of port exhaustion per address. An example scenario is an organization with a small block of public IPs that wants to spread outbound translation across those addresses for capacity or policy reasons. In Junos you define a source rule-set that matches traffic and then specify a source-nat pool instead of interface. A common misconception is that pool NAT provides privacy or security benefits beyond address diversity; it mainly affects capacity and how remote servers see your origin addresses. When troubleshooting, ensure your match conditions (such as source-address) accurately reflect the internal networks you intended to translate. If you forget to restrict matches, you may accidentally translate traffic you did not intend to, which complicates logging and tracing. Pool NAT and when to use it means pool nat maps internal addresses to a range of public ips for better scaling and distribution of outbound traffic.. In practical terms, distributing translations across multiple public ip addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Destination NAT, often called port forwarding, changes the destination IP and optionally the destination port of incoming packets so external users reach an internal server. A common use case is exposing a web server in a DMZ: external clients connect to a public IP on port 80, and the NAT device translates that destination to the internal web server's private IP and port. It's important to pair DNAT with a security policy that permits the translated destination; NAT alone does not open a path. For example, if you translate 203.0.113.5:80 to 192.168.1.10:80, you still need a Junos policy from the untrust zone to the dmz zone that allows HTTP to 192.168.1.10. A common misconception is to use source-address any in DNAT rules; restricting match conditions by destination-port and destination-address reduces exposure. Also, be precise with zones; misconfigured from/to zones prevents the DNAT rule from being applied. After configuration, verify translations with show security nat destination and inspect sessions with show security flow session to confirm the translation and policy match. In practical terms, mapping public ip and port to an internal server. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between a private IP and a public IP. This is useful for servers that must be consistently reachable at an unchanging public address, such as mail or legacy systems that rely on fixed source IPs. Because the mapping is static, there is no port translation by default; the public IP is always mapped to the same private host. A typical mistake is to use static NAT for hosts that could instead be protected behind DNAT and selective port forwarding; static NAT increases exposure because the mapped public address resolves directly to the internal host. When configuring static NAT on Junos, ensure access is limited by security policy and that DNS and external services are updated to reference the assigned public address. Verify mappings with show security nat destination for DNAT-like scenarios or by checking the NAT rule-set and confirming traffic flows using show security flow session after initiating connections.
